## The math and its two criteria

Kelly says you must meet two criteria.

1. **Enough output to earn about $100 profit per true fan per year.** He equates this to one day's wages per year from each fan. It is easier in some fields than others, but he argues it is always easier and better to give existing customers more than to find new fans.
2. **A direct relationship.** Fans must pay you directly, so you keep all of it rather than the small percentage you would get from a label, publisher, studio or retailer.

Then the arithmetic is just:

$$1{,}000 \text{ fans} \times \$100 = \$100{,}000 \text{ per year}$$

The 2008 version states the same assumption, notes that $100 is an average because the truest fans spend a lot more, and subtracts "some modest expenses". The number 1,000 is not sacred: it is a rough order of magnitude, three orders below a million. At $50 per fan you need 2,000; at $200, 500. If you only need $75K a year, you need fewer.
